description: We're a group of university students, mostly studying computer engineering, with backgrounds that also cover aerospace and civil engineering, management, data science and game development. We joined Space Apps to work on a real problem together and see what we can build by combining what each of us knows. Between us we cover software, data, engineering and project planning, and we're looking forward to putting that to use on one of this year's challenges.
summary:
Astronodes is a cooperative multiplayer browser game in which a team runs a small space program. Players walk around a space center in first person, read the mission brief in the Lab, assemble a rocket in a full-size hangar, roll it out to the pad and fly it by hand, from the ground to space.

No flight is an animation. Our own simulator computes each one from published equations: inverse-square gravity on a rotating Earth, the U.S. Standard Atmosphere 1976, the rocket thrust equation, shock-wave and Prandtl–Meyer relations for supersonic drag, Barrowman stability and Sutton–Graves heating (NASA TR R-376), integrated with fourth-order Runge–Kutta. A rocket fails for a physical reason: it overheats, tumbles, bursts its motor case or lands too hard. A flight report explains what went wrong and how to fix it.

This is how the game addresses the challenge. Each launch costs money, so the team must balance mass, cost, thrust, stability, heat protection and recovery. Controls and telemetry are split between two roles, so the crew has to talk each flight through over voice and text chat. Players learn why missions succeed or fail the way engineers do: by testing a design, reading the data and improving it.
details:
What does it do?

Astronodes is a cooperative multiplayer game that runs in a desktop browser with nothing to install. A crew of up to five players joins a room with a six-character code, picks an astronaut and a role, and runs a small space program together: one rocket, one budget and one launch history. A single player can also play solo and hold both roles. The crew designs a rocket to fulfill a mission, pays for it, flies it by hand and reads why the flight ended the way it did. Then it improves the design and flies again.

How does it work?

Players walk around a space center in first person, see each other's astronauts and talk over built-in voice and text chat. Each building is one part of the mission:

  • Lab: the mission brief, goals and bonus challenges, research to buy, and the launch history. The campaign has ten missions, from a first 1 km flight to carrying a 2 kg payload to 100 km and landing it safely. Completed missions earn knowledge points, which unlock new parts and materials.
  • Hangar: Players assemble the launch vehicle part by part and enter dimensions and wall thicknesses numerically where applicable. They select construction materials and heat shield types for compatible parts, specify nozzle throat and exit diameters, and define solid propellant grain geometry by its outer diameter, initial bore diameter, and length. Liquid stages can be configured with up to 19 engines in a cluster.
  • Satellite Building: a satellite is built from a frame, solar panels, antennas, cameras, a battery and other parts, then carried in the rocket's satellite compartment.
  • Rocket Control: the launch checklist, paid ground tests (static fire, drop test, wind tunnel), roll-out to the pad, a 10-second countdown and the flight console. The astronaut starts and stops the engine, drops stages, steers with movable fins and opens the parachute. Nothing happens by itself after lift-off.
  • Communication Center: the only place that shows flight numbers. Altitude, speed, Mach number, forces, fuel left per stage, heat warnings, a live rocket camera and a whole-Earth map with the predicted trajectory.

Two roles split the information. The Builder/Astronaut builds and flies the rocket but does not see the numbers. Ground Control sees the limits and the live flight data and tells the astronaut what to do and when. Telemetry only arrives if the rocket carries a flight computer, a battery and a telemetry unit, so communications are part of the design.

After every flight a report lists the goals met, the money earned and what went wrong, in plain words. If a rocket carries a satellite onto a closed orbit, the satellite is released and the crew watches it circle the Earth, with the Moon at its true size and distance.

Scientific basis

Our own flight simulator computes every flight from published equations. Nothing in a flight is scripted: the outcome follows from the rocket the team built.

  • Dynamics: a 3D trajectory in an Earth-centred inertial frame on a rotating spherical Earth, launched from a real site (Andøya Spaceport, Norway). Inverse-square gravity, drag on air-relative velocity, fourth-order Runge–Kutta integration.
  • Attitude: a rigid body in pitch and yaw. Centre of mass and moment of inertia are recomputed as propellant burns and stages separate. Barrowman normal-force coefficients with a compressibility correction give the static margin the builder checks.
  • Atmosphere and Aerodynamics: The game models Earth’s atmosphere using the U.S. Standard Atmosphere (1976) up to 1,000 km. It estimates drag from subsonic to hypersonic flight using the rocket’s assembled geometry, including its nose profile and changes in diameter between stages. The aerodynamic model combines Reynolds-number-dependent skin friction with pressure drag estimates based on normal and oblique shock relations, Prandtl–Meyer expansion, and modified Newtonian theory. As the atmosphere thins, it blends from continuum to rarefied-flow drag using the Knudsen number.
  • Propulsion: solid motors with grain regression and a chamber-pressure balance; the rocket thrust equation with an ideal nozzle at every flow condition, including a shock inside an over-expanded nozzle; throttleable, restartable liquid engines.
  • Heating: a temperature for each surface. Sutton–Graves stagnation-point heating at the nose (NASA TR R-376), Reynolds-analogy heating on the body, radiative cooling, and ablative heat shields that lose mass as they burn away.
  • Orbit: apogee, perigee, inclination, period and impact point from the state vector.
  • Failures: overheating, a motor case bursting under chamber pressure (thin-wall hoop stress), aerodynamic instability and a hard landing.
  • Parts: each part's mass is its shell volume times the material's density.

The simulator has about 100 automated tests that check it against reference values: rows of the standard atmosphere table, worked nozzle and drag cases, mass conservation through a burn, a circular orbit that stays circular, and results that do not change with the time step. Further tests fly a reference rocket for every mission, so every goal is proven reachable.

What benefits does it have?

  • Players learn by doing. A failed flight is explained in words for free, and exact limits come from ground tests or research the team pays for, as in a real program.
  • Every choice has a price. A launch costs the rocket's price and a safe landing refunds half, so players weigh mass, cost, thrust, stability, heat protection and recovery.
  • It trains teamwork. Neither role can complete a flight alone.
  • It is easy to reach: a link, a room code and a desktop browser.

What is the intended impact?

We want students and space enthusiasts to experience the design, test and improve loop of mission engineering, and to see that real rockets fail for reasons that can be understood and fixed. History cards connect the missions to Goddard's 1926 rocket, Bumper-WAC in 1949 and Freedom 7 in 1961.

What tools, coding languages, hardware or software did you use?

  • Languages: TypeScript (strict), HTML and CSS; Python for the sound export script.
  • 3D rendering: Three.js with react-three-fiber, drei and postprocessing.
  • Interface: React with our own design system.
  • Simulation: our own package in pure TypeScript, with no dependencies.
  • Multiplayer: Firebase Realtime Database behind our own sync package, with an offline local mode; WebRTC for voice chat.
  • Build, test and deployment: Vite, Vitest, npm workspaces, GitHub Actions and Firebase Hosting.
  • Data and assets: NASA imagery for the Earth and the Moon, Google Fonts, and procedural 3D art built in code.
  • AI tools: AI coding assistants (Claude, ChatGPT).
  • Hardware: none beyond a computer with a desktop browser, keyboard and mouse; a microphone is optional.

How is your project creative?

  • Controls and telemetry are in different buildings, which turns communication into a game mechanic.
  • The space center is a place to walk through together, not a menu. The hangar and the launch pad are real size.
  • Components are tailored, not picked from a fixed list. Parts can be scaled up to 100× and rockets up to 110 m, following the square-cube law, and the game shows the effect on height, mass, cost and thrust-to-weight before a change is applied.
  • The view goes from the launch pad to space and back without a cut, over a full-scale Earth.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Accuracy against playability: we used real equations and NASA data, and labelled every simplified or estimated value as such.
  • Fair multiplayer: one browser runs the simulation and shares it, so every player sees the same flight.
  • Cost: only free and open-source tools and free hosting.
  • Accessibility: the game respects the system's reduced-motion setting, supports keyboard focus and has quality levels for slower computers.
  • Rules: no NASA logos or insignia in the game, and sources recorded for real-world values.

Use of AI tools

Most of the code, the procedural 3D art and the documentation were written with AI coding assistants, directed, reviewed and tested by the team. The game itself contains no AI: the flight report is rule-based. Earth and Moon textures are NASA imagery, only resized or converted.
